Applied Ergonomics

Volume 119, September 2024, 104319

Development of a virtual reality system usability questionnaire (VRSUQ)

Author links open overlay panel,
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apergo.2024.104319Get rights and content

Abstract

Virtual reality (VR) has gained significant attention as a technology that provides immersive experiences similar to the real world. In order for a VR system to be accepted, usability needs to be guaranteed. Accordingly, VR-related researchers are continuing their efforts to improve VR systems by conducting usability evaluations. However, existing studies have limitations in that they cannot comprehensively evaluate the detailed properties of VR systems by using questionnaires developed for general product usability evaluation or focusing only on some usability aspects of VR systems. This suggests it may be difficult to fully capture usability issues in a VR system, and that it is necessary to develop a usability evaluation tool that reflects the specific characteristics of the VR system. Therefore, this study develops and proposes the Virtual Reality System Usability Questionnaire (VRSUQ). In the development of the questionnaire, items were structured based on a literature review and discussions with experts. To account for the diverse characteristics of VR systems, the validity of the questionnaire was verified through both exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis, utilizing data obtained from three distinct experimental studies that employed different VR systems. In addition, by comparing the results of VRSUQ with the results from the System Usability Scale, which is widely used for perceived usability evaluation, alternative possibilities for using VRSUQ are presented. Further testing on various VR platforms is needed to ensure the reliability and validity of VRSUQ, and as results from using VRSUQ are accumulated, it is expected to be widely used as a more powerful and robust VR-specific perceived usability evaluation tool.

Virtual reality
Usability evaluation

1. Introduction

Virtual Reality (VR) is a computer technology that allows users to experience immersion in a digital environment that is either similar to the real world or entirely created. It provides a three-dimensional spatially immersive environment, making users feel as if they are present within that space (Jerald, 2015). Also, VR achieves this experience through visual, auditory, and sometimes tactile feedback. On the other hand, a VR system is the integrated combination of hardware, software, and interfaces required to create and deliver these VR experiences. A VR system includes a variety of devices such as specially designed headsets, motion sensors, gloves, haptic devices, etc., that allow users to freely move, manipulate objects, and interact within the virtual environment (Kalawsky, 1999; Kim et al., 2020). This system offers a highly interactive and spatially immersive experience, going beyond mere VR experiences to enable users to have experiences akin to real life. In other words, a VR system acts as a specialized human-computer interface that enables interaction between the user and the virtual environment, making it essential for realizing the VR experience.

Depending on the level of immersion, it is largely classified into non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive VR (Burdea and Coiffet, 2003), and development to provide a higher immersive experience has been continuously made. Representative fully immersive VR types include head-mounted display (HMD)-based VR systems and Cave Automatic Virtual Environment (CAVE). Recently, with the advent of the term metaverse, the concept of VR has become popular, its scope has been expanded, and the global metaverse market is expected to grow to approximately US$1.3 trillion by 2030 (Precedence Research, 2023). As new VR-related services and contents expand in line with the popularization of the metaverse and its market growth, related technologies are expected to advance, and opportunities for the general public to experience VR are expected to increase.

Human-computer interaction (HCI) researchers in both academia and industry have placed importance on the usability of products. Products with high usability are more likely to succeed because users find them easy and convenient (Rhiu and Yun, 2018). Therefore, it is important to seek a certain level of usability rather than focusing only on technological development. In addition, when a new product is developed or improved, or when a new interaction is applied to a product, efforts are made to make it more convenient through usability evaluation (Kim et al., 2018, 2020). In particular, VR has very diverse components, so new interactions are applied, and users can experience a variety of VR content even in the same configuration. Thus, VR usability issues should be continuously addressed in order for the system to be accepted.

In previous studies, questionnaires that reflected the characteristics of specific products were developed to evaluate their perceived usability. For example, several studies developed usability evaluation questionnaires specific to systems like mobile phone user interfaces (Ji et al., 2006), mobile health care applications (Zhou et al., 2019), mobile commerce applications (Ajibola and Goosen, 2017), and online education (Zaharias and Poylymenakou, 2009). Developing a usability evaluation tool for a specific product is important for several reasons. Usability evaluation metrics should be selected and developed by considering specific contexts of use and product characteristics (functions, interactions, etc.). For example, merely evaluating usability at a general level, such as efficiency, effectiveness, or satisfaction, may not adequately capture the unique characteristics of a particular product. Product-specific usability evaluation tools are designed to measure the most important aspects of that product to obtain more reliable results. Therefore, usability evaluation tools that reflect a particular product's characteristics can provide deeper insight into the user experience, helping to identify areas for improvement and ways to make the right decisions.

In this context, in order to identify important issues in VR systems and improve usability, it is necessary to develop evaluation tools that reflect VR characteristics. Virtual environments (VEs) provide an immersive experience compared to traditional computer systems, and the way users interact with them is fundamentally different than in a typical computer interface. For example, VR systems often use a combination of handheld controllers, an HMD, and other input devices to allow users to interact with the 3D environment (Kim et al., 2020). Therefore, it might be necessary to consider and reflect these unique interaction methods in the VR-only usability dimension. In addition, despite the efforts to develop VR system standardization, such as ISO/IEC 23842–1 (ISO/IEC TR 23842-1:2020, 2020) and ISO/IEC 23842–2 (ISO/IEC TR 23842-2:2020, 2020), there is still a lack of standardization, so various VR systems use a variety of hardware, software, content, and interaction methods. Therefore, by developing a universal evaluation tool for VR systems, usability can be compared and managed by evaluating existing VR systems and newly developed VR systems from the same dimensions. Consequently, developing a VR-specific usability evaluation tool is important to ensure a positive VR experience and to guide the design and development of VR technology in a way that meets the unique needs and expectations of VR users.

Efforts have been made to structure metrics and develop questionnaires to evaluate the perceived usability of VR systems. For example, Kalawsky (1999) developed a questionnaire to measure the perceived usability of a VR system according to the user's attitude and perception (VRUSE). Kalawsky (1999) stated that VR systems are characterized by providing users with immersion and presence, and they require a high level of interactivity compared to conventional computer systems, emphasizing that these aspects should be considered in the usability evaluation of VR systems. Based on this motivation, a usability evaluation tool for VR was developed, and a total of 10 usability factors were presented (functionality, user input, system output, user guidance and help, consistency, flexibility, simulation fidelity, error correction/handling and robustness, sense of immersion/presence, and overall system usability). VRUSE has the advantage of being able to evaluate the usability of a VR system from various aspects, but information on the results of scale reliability and construct validity for each factor was not presented. In addition, since the 10 usability factors consist of 100 individual items, there is the possibility of causing fatigue in participants when comparing various experimental conditions.

Stanney et al. (2003) developed the Multi-criteria Assessment of Usability for Virtual Environments (MAUVE) to consider the perceived usability of a VR system from various aspects. They proposed criteria for usability evaluation of virtual environments based on the differences between GUI-based traditional computer systems and VR systems. Through an extensive literature review, the usability characteristics of VEs are largely divided into system interfaces and user interfaces. System interfaces constitute elements of interactions (i.e., navigation, wayfinding, and object manipulation) and multimodal system output (i.e., visual, haptic, and auditory). In user interfaces, engagement and side effects are selected as the main factors. MAUVE has an evaluation step that assigns a weight to each element, so the importance of each one can be identified. However, since the number of individual items for each element ranges from 4 to 34, participants’ fatigue could increase when usability evaluation for various conditions has to be performed. When this is a concern, it may be difficult to secure reliability in the results. Furthermore, although individual items for each element were constructed through a literature review, a limitation is that results proving validity of the constructs were not presented.

Sutcliffe and Gault (2004) proposed 12 heuristics for usability inspection of VR applications based on heuristic evaluation by Nielsen (1994). The evaluation method proposed has the characteristics of a heuristic evaluation method, so it has the advantages of quick evaluation and cost effectiveness. The proposed heuristics include natural engagement, compatibility, natural expression of action, close coordination of action and representation, realistic feedback, faithful viewpoints, navigation and orientation support, clear entry and exit points, consistent departures, support for learning, clear turn-taking, and a sense of presence. A case study suggests that the proposed heuristics successfully detect usability problems in a VE, but there are some limitations. First of all, as the authors noted, overlap was found among the heuristics items assessing natural interactions. Experts who are proficient in both VR systems and usability evaluation can recognize the subtle differences, but practitioners who lack background knowledge need a higher level of understanding, which may require separate learning sessions. In addition, evaluation items for positive experiences that VR should provide to users, such as engagement and presence, are included, but negative experiences such as motion sickness, workload, and stress caused by VR experiences were not considered in the evaluation.

Efforts to develop usability evaluation metrics for VR systems have continued in recent years, reflecting the need to address the unique experiences and challenges of VR systems. Rusu et al. (2011) addressed the need for new evaluation methods in the rapidly expanding space of Virtual Worlds (VWs). The study proposed a set of 16 specific usability heuristics and an associated usability checklist, highlighting the balance between specificity and generality to enhance usability evaluations of VW applications. Gil-Gómez et al. (2013) introduced a novel questionnaire designed for virtual rehabilitation systems, emphasizing usability, acceptance, and security. This tool is based on the short feedback questionnaire (Kizony et al., 2003) but includes additional questions to cover fundamental items not addressed by the original questionnaire, showing promising preliminary results in terms of internal consistency and initial suitability evaluation. Similarly, Gil-Gómez et al. (2017) presented a questionnaire focused on evaluating user satisfaction within virtual rehabilitation systems. Initial findings suggest that the User Satisfaction Evaluation Questionnaire (USEQ) is a reliable tool with adequate internal consistency, designed to capture the specific needs and satisfaction levels of patients using VR for balance disorders rehabilitation. Furthermore, a study on the development of a usability evaluation tool for VR platforms highlights the need for new evaluation elements and interfaces from a user's perspective, distinct from those used in traditional platform usability evaluations (Chung and Jang, 2019). By examining current VR platforms and utilizing the Delphi technique, the study identified 33 evaluation items grouped into eight factors, offering a comprehensive tool for evaluating VR content search and purchase processes on VR platforms.

These studies represent significant progress in the development of usability measurement tools for VR, contributing to solving the unique challenges of VR environments and providing a framework for the more effective evaluation of VR applications and systems. However, they also highlight the limitations in developing comprehensive and universally applicable metrics within the diverse and rapidly evolving field of virtual reality. As a result, despite efforts to develop usability evaluation questionnaires that capture the distinct characteristics of VR systems, these tools have not achieved widespread adoption or been recognized as standard benchmarks for assessing the usability of VR applications. According to Kim et al. (2020), well-structured usability questionnaires that can be applied to general products, but that are not dedicated to VR, are frequently used to evaluate the usability of VR systems. Among them, the System Usability Scale (SUS) (Brooke, 1996) has become the most popular, and is applied to perceived usability evaluations of various VR systems such as HMD-based and screen-based VR and CAVE (Brade et al., 2017; Ni et al., 2014; Pick et al., 2016).

The SUS has been adapted to evaluate the usability of various VR systems by modifying its questions to better reflect the specific characteristics and contexts of each experiment. By adjusting the term "system" to the specific VR system being evaluated, it enables a comprehensive consideration of the context information that the VR system includes, such as the combination of interaction methods, hardware configurations, and tasks. The widespread use of SUS can be attributed fundamentally to the inherent advantages that SUS offers. First, SUS consists of relatively few items, so a quick evaluation is possible (Tullis and Stetson, 2004). Second, usability evaluation between comparison objects is possible by deriving a standard SUS score (Brooke, 1996), and interpretation at an absolute level based on a specific score is also possible based on a curved grading scale suggested by Sauro and Lewis (2016). Furthermore, several previous studies showed that SUS has high reliability, validity, and sensitivity (Sauro and Lewis, 2016). Nonetheless, this strategy can be seen as arising due to the absence of a widely validated usability evaluation tool that is specialized for virtual reality systems. To bridge this gap and ensure that usability assessments are aligned with the unique situations and experiences of VR systems, the development of dedicated usability evaluation tools specifically designed to consider the characteristics of VR systems is necessary.

The SUS has been developed as a critical tool for measuring the usability of products or services. This questionnaire evaluates ease of use and user satisfaction to improve the intuitiveness and accessibility of products or services. The development of SUS was initiated as part of efforts to standardize usability evaluation and provide a rapid and cost-effective method. Subsequent research has continuously verified the validity and robustness of the SUS. Borsci et al. (2009) tested alternative measurement models for the dimensionality of SUS, deepening the understanding of the questionnaire's structural validity. Lewis and Sauro (2009) enhanced the reliability and applicability of the questionnaire through their study on the factor structure of SUS. The results of these studies suggested that the SUS could be a two-dimensional measurement consisting of usability and learnability (Borsci et al., 2009; Lewis and Sauro, 2009). Also, Finstad, (2010) expanded the utility of SUS by proposing a new metric for usability measurement, the Usability Metric for User Experience (UMUX). In 2013, Lewis, Utesch, and Maher introduced UMUX-LITE, developing a concise and reliable tool that could substitute SUS in situations where time is limited. This effort aimed at increasing the efficiency of usability evaluation while simplifying the assessment process. Lewis and Sauro conducted a confirmatory factor analysis, thereby providing a deep analysis of the dimensionality of SUS across thousands of cases (Lewis and Sauro, 2017). The results of this study provided strong evidence for the use of SUS as a one-dimensional measure, serving as one of the key reasons Lewis (2018b) advocated for its application in this way. This recommendation was highlighted in his comprehensive review of the past, present, and future of SUS, marking it as a significant piece of research supporting the one-dimensional use of SUS.

However, even if SUS is an advantageous and powerful tool for evaluating usability in one or two dimensions, a tool that comprehensively evaluates perceived usability may still be needed. In addition, it is questionable whether SUS can be used as an evaluation tool for perceived usability of VR, because it was not developed considering the specifics of a VR system. As a simple example, SUS and subsequent versions of SUS do not include evaluation indicators such as immersion, presence, and discomfort, which constitute a user's subjective satisfaction. For this reason, several previous studies evaluated VR experiences from various aspects by simultaneously utilizing well-structured questionnaires that can evaluate presence (e.g., ITC-SOPI, PQ, and IPQ), motion sickness (e.g., SSQ and VRSQ), and workload (e.g., NASA-TLX and the Borg scale) in addition to usability questionnaires like SUS. However, considering that most VR experimental studies are based on fragmentary experiences lasting a relatively short time due to side effects such as HMD weight (Bowman et al., 2002; Won et al., 2022) and simulator motion sickness.

To evaluate the usability of a VR system's multifaceted elements, Winter et al. (2021) considered pleasure, presence, motion sickness, and workload as important factors. They used intrinsic motivation inventory (45 items), the iGroup presence questionnaire (14 items), a simulator sickness questionnaire (16 items), a raw task load index (6 items), and the Borg scale. Their findings indicate that when evaluating the usability of a VE, it is necessary to consider indicators from various aspects at the same time (such as motion sickness, pleasure, and presence), going beyond simply evaluating whether the system can be used easily and conveniently. However, considering that the VR experience lasted less than 7.5 min, the 82 questionnaire items could have caused unintentional fatigue in the participants, and accordingly, it is questionable whether it was possible to secure reliable data.

Therefore, the purpose of this study is to develop the Virtual Reality System Usability Questionnaire (VRSUQ) by identifying and structuring usability evaluation indicators that can evaluate VR from various perspectives by considering VR characteristics.

2. Development of the VRSUQ

The development procedure for VRSUQ to comprehensively evaluate the perceived usability of VR was divided into 1) the measurement derivation stage, and 2) the measurement development stage. In the first stage, the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) method was applied for systematic literature analysis, and the task of structuring the derived individual indicators was carried out through expert workshops.

2.1. Measurement derivation

2.1.1. Information source and inclusion criteria

We derived perceived usability evaluation measurements based on a systematic literature analysis of five academic databases: Scopus, Web of Science, Science Direct, ACM Digital Library, and ProQuest. For the review, only journal articles in English were chosen, while brief reports, news articles, conference proceedings, books, and dissertations were omitted. Articles were searched using keywords for virtual reality (virtual reality OR virtual environment), usability evaluation (usability evaluation OR usability testing), and HMD (head-mounted display OR HMD). Additionally, considering the focus on widely accessible and extensively distributed VR systems, we specifically targeted HMD-based VR systems, which represent a significant segment of fully immersive VR systems easily accessible to the public (Kim et al., 2020).

2.1.2. Eligibility criteria

Papers were selected after a thorough reading process, focusing on those that evaluated usability as a mandatory assessment element for HMD-based VR systems and presented usability-related metrics. Consequently, the selected research must (1) utilize HMD-based VR systems and (2) evaluate the usability of these VR systems. Beyond these two criteria, there were no restrictions regarding the type of VR system, characteristics of participants, research design, or evaluation methods in the paper selection process.

2.1.3. Study selection

The review process and the number of papers selected at each stage are detailed in Fig. 1, beginning with the initial collection of 188 papers through keyword searches. Following the removal of duplicates across databases, the count was narrowed down to 169 papers, and a subsequent preliminary review process further reduced this number to 31. Ultimately, after a meticulous evaluation against the eligibility criteria, 16 papers were selected for inclusion.

2.1.4. Usability evaluation indexes

To evaluate the perceived usability of HMD-based VR systems, well-structured questionnaires from various fields or self-developed questionnaires were used, depending on the purpose of the study from a broad perspective. In particular, SUS is well-established as a commonly used questionnaire (Ferracani et al., 2017; Avola et al., 2019; Huang, 2020; Rhiu et al., 2020; Zorzal et al., 2021; Winter et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021). In other words, SUS has been frequently adopted as a questionnaire on the perceived usability of VEs, even though it was not developed solely to evaluate them. Even when self-developed questionnaire items were used, the usability of the VR system was evaluated from various aspects. The usability evaluation measurements used in each previous study are presented in Table 1.

2.2. Framework of the perceived usability dimensions

The concept of usability may differ depending on the products and systems developed by researchers and practitioners participating in HCI and usability engineering, but basically, usability dimensions presented by ISO 9241–11:2018 are accepted without much disagreement. ISO 9241-11:2018 (2018) defines usability as “The effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction with which specified users achieve specified goals in particular environments.” According to that definition, and based on these criteria, we propose a usability questionnaire framework for evaluation of VR.

In this study, VRSUQ was structured according to the above three dimensions of usability described by ISO and it was developed according to the following procedure. In order to evaluate whether each measurement is suitable for use in VR evaluation based on a sufficient understanding of each one, five HCI experts in the VR field participated, evaluating the similarity and importance of each measurement. Initially, the experts conducted a comprehensive review to identify measurements with overlapping meanings or similar expressions, focusing on consolidating these into unified metrics. For instance, the concepts of “Dizziness,” “Nausea,” and “Sea-sickness” were amalgamated into the singular measurement of “Motion sickness,” reflecting a concerted effort to capture the essence of physical discomfort experienced in VR. Subsequently, among the measurements with closely related definitions, the experts selected representative metrics that best encapsulated the underlying concepts, ensuring the questionnaire's relevance and precision. An example of this can be seen in the decision to consolidate “Complexity” and “Easy to use” into “Learnability,” emphasizing the importance of intuitive learning in the VR experience. Moreover, in the final phase of the VRSUQ's development, the experts carefully considered the distinctive characteristics of HMD-based VR systems, tailoring the measurements to accurately reflect the immersive and interactive nature of these experiences. This step involved a nuanced differentiation between the positive and negative experiences derived from VR usage. Positive aspects, such as the sensations of “Being there” and “Happy,” were collectively categorized under the measurement of "Pleasure" to accurately capture the range of positive emotional and experiential outcomes facilitated by VR environments. Concurrently, the framework addressed physical and emotional discomforts as separate considerations, ensuring a comprehensive evaluation of the user experience. Throughout the process, measurements were combined, removed, or categorized only if at least 4 out of 5 experts agreed. Through this process, VRSUQ was structured to include three unique measurements for each of the three usability dimensions described by ISO, completing it as a tool designed to evaluate the multifaceted usability of VR systems (Table 2).

Effectiveness refers to the ability of a system to achieve its intended goals with accuracy and completeness, so an effective system is one that enables users to successfully complete tasks with minimal errors. The effectiveness dimension includes three evaluation measurements. Compatibility refers to the degree to which the system's behavior and response match the user's expectations, and how consistent they are with the real-world objects or interactions they represent. In virtual reality, a manipulation method needs to match the user's expectations for the real object as much as possible, and reaction to the manipulation also needs to match in order to provide compatibility. For example, if a user is trying to grab and move a virtual object, the system should respond in a way that matches the user's expected result based on their real-world experience with similar objects. In other words, VR systems should provide a user interface that is intuitive and easy to navigate, and the interactions with virtual objects should feel natural and similar to the real-world counterparts. Feedback refers to the information that a system provides to users about their actions, progress, or errors. In VR systems, effective feedback can help users understand their movements and interactions within the VE and can guide them towards completing their goals. For example, a VR game that provides visual or auditory feedback when a user completes a task or receives points can enhance the effectiveness of the overall experience. Error prevention refers to the degree to which a system is designed to minimize or eliminate errors that users may encounter. For example, a VR application that includes warning messages or safety features to prevent users from accidently walking into walls or objects in the real world can enhance the overall effectiveness of the system.

In terms of efficiency, VR systems should allow users to accomplish their objectives with a minimum of time, effort, and resources. In the context of VR systems, efficiency can be measured by three factors: understandability, learnability, and error recovery. Understandability is the degree to which users can comprehend and interpret the information presented within the VE. A highly understandable system ensures that users can easily identify and comprehend the various elements, controls, and functions without confusion or ambiguity. For example, a VR system that displays clear and concise instructions or visual cues to guide users towards the next step of a task can be considered highly understandable. Learnability refers to the degree to which users can quickly and easily learn to use the VR system. A highly learnable system is intuitive and user-friendly, with clear and concise instructions and minimal steps required to perform tasks. For example, a VR system that uses natural and intuitive gestures or movements to control actions rather than complex button presses or keyboard commands can be considered highly learnable. Error recovery is how easily a user can recover from an error that occurred during a VR experience. A system with efficient error recovery features allows users to quickly and easily correct mistakes, without losing any progress or data.

Satisfaction refers to the extent to which users find a system useful, effective, efficient, and satisfying. In this regard, VR should provide a pleasant and satisfying experience that leaves users feeling positive about their interaction with the system. Three measurements were identified as important factors of satisfaction. Pleasure refers to the degree to which users enjoy using system. A pleasurable experience can increase user engagement and satisfaction, leading to better task performance. Motion sickness in VR systems could occur when visual perception does not match physical movements, resulting in a feeling of dizziness or nausea. This is especially common in VR systems that involve fast or jerky movements, such as roller coaster simulators. Motion sickness can negatively impact user performance and satisfaction, leading to a decreased willingness to use the system. Emotional discomfort in VR refers to negative emotional responses such as tension, frustration, and time pressure. This can occur when the system is difficult to use, if the user is unable to complete a task within a given amount of time, or when the system causes anxiety or fear.

3. Method

To validate the VRSUQ, we conducted a series of three experiments, each utilizing a different HMD-based VR system. Although all systems were based on HMDs, they varied significantly in their primary tasks and interaction modalities. The first experiment (E1) focused on a flat terrain navigation task using gesture controls. The second experiment (E2) involved a navigation task that utilized an omnidirectional treadmill, offering a more immersive experience in moving through virtual environments. The third experiment (E3) was centered on manipulation tasks using handheld controllers, emphasizing precision and interaction within the VR space. These experiments were strategically devised to comprehensively reflect the spectrum of VR systems across diverse contexts and detailed descriptions of each experiment will be provided in the following sections on methods.

3.1. Participants

A total of 103 participants with no physical or mental health problems participated in this study (54 males, 49 females, mean age = 22.75 ± 2.12). All but six participants had experience with 3D stereoscopic images, and 52 participants had experience with HMD-based VR systems. The information for all participants, as well as the detailed participant information for each experiment, is presented in Table 3.

3.2. VR systems, virtual environments, interaction methods, and tasks

The experiments E1 through E3 utilized the same head-mounted display (HMD) devices and personal computers (PCs). The VR device employed was the HTC Corporation VIVE Pro Eye, an HMD-based VR system. This HMD offers high-resolution visuals at 1440 × 1600 pixels per eye, along with a 110° field of view, providing an immersive experience for the user. Additionally, it is equipped with integrated headphones to deliver auditory feedback directly, eliminating the need for separate earphones. The PC setup included an Intel Core i9-10850K CPU running at 3.60 GHz, an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 graphics card, and 32 GB of RAM, ensuring high performance and smooth operation of the VR applications used in the experiments. The play area for E1 and E3 was 2.5 m × 2.5 m, satisfying the recommended minimum of 2 m × 1.5 m. For E2, Virtuix Omni treadmill was used, negating the need for an additional room-scale setup.

In E1, all participants navigated the same path using walking in place (WIP) locomotion. This method allows users to infinitely move through the virtual reality environment with a natural walk while remaining stationary (Slater et al., 1995). Because this method closely simulates actual walking, it can enhance user immersion in the virtual reality environment. (Feasel et al., 2008; LaViola et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2020; Kim and Rhiu, 2021; Kim et al., 2021). For a navigation task, we used Simple Town implemented in the Freedom Locomotion VR (released March 13, 2017) and performed on SteamVR. The participant was asked to navigate a predefined path, consisting of a simple route including a left turn, a right turn, and walking straight ahead (Fig. 2). The task was completed when the participant returned to the starting position. The participants were asked to return as soon as possible without colliding with obstacles (e.g., cars and pillars).

In E2, participants utilized the Omni treadmill platform, enabling navigation in all directions through WIP gestures (Fig. 3). The VR content, named TRAVR: Training Ops, was employed, focusing on navigation tasks as the core activity. Participants aimed to reach their destinations as swiftly as possible and were instructed to follow a marked path on the floor, ignoring game obstacles such as lasers and OX targets. Additionally, participants were asked to walk at their natural walking speed without running and to stay as close to the center of the marked path as possible. Similar to E1, the path included straight movements, right and left turns, and additionally incorporated various terrains such as ascending and descending stairs, following a predetermined route.

In E3, the primary task was set to manipulate virtual objects. Utilizing the content LabTrainingVR: Personal Protective Equipment Edition, which runs on SteamVR, participants were required to perform various manipulation tasks using handheld controllers in both hands (Fig. 4). Positioned within a virtual laboratory, participants needed to wear equipment such as goggles, lab coats, and gloves. Also, the task involved retrieving specific objects from a locker, moving them to another location, and then discarding all worn equipment into a trash bin. Compared to E1 and E2, E3 demanded diverse 3D manipulations, and the accompanying navigation was implemented through teleportation, differing from the locomotion methods used in E1 and E2.

3.3. Perceived usability measurement and procedures

The entire experimental procedure was the same for all experiments and was composed of three phases (Fig. 5). First was preparation, in which the size of the HMD was adjusted to fit the participant's head. The first stage was preparation, during which the size of the HMD was adjusted to fit the participant's head. Additionally, in E2, participants were equipped with Omni treadmill-specific shoes and wore a harness structure for upper body support. VR content was executed, and the focal length and eye level were calibrated. In addition, the participant attended a training session to get accustomed to the locomotion interface and manipulation methods. In the second phase (the experiment), the given task was explained, and participants executed it using the movement and manipulation interfaces. After completing the tasks, the questionnaire session was conducted. In it, participants completed the VRSUQ (Appendix A), SUS (Appendix A), and the demographics section. Both questionnaires adopted a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree). For experiments E1, E2, and E3, the average time taken for each experiment was 5.67, 5.48, and 6.10 min, respectively. Additionally, it took an average of less than 3 min to complete each of the surveys for VRSUQ and SUS, respectively.

3.4. Statistical analysis

We first confirmed the internal consistency of the VRSUQ using Cronbach's alpha values. To validate the construct validity, we conducted both exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses. For the exploratory factor analysis (EFA), we utilized principal axis factoring extraction. The confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was performed using the R programming environment (Version 4.0.5), employing the ‘lavaan’ package for this purpose. Furthermore, to verify convergent validity, we derived VRSUQ scores corresponding to the SUS scores and analyzed the bivariate correlation between these two sets of scores. After confirming the reliability and validity of the VRSUQ, we described its utility by performing a one-way repeated-measures ANOVA (RM-ANOVA) for each factor of the VRSUQ to further explore the evaluation results. Negative-toned items (e.g., physical and emotional discomfort) were reverse-coded prior to statistical analysis. In other words, for all items, higher scores are more positive. All analyses, with the exception of the CFA, were conducted using SPSS (Version 27.0). The statistical significance level for all analyses was set at 0.05. An overview of all statistical analysis methods and procedures is presented in Fig. 6.

4. Results

4.1. Scale reliability

The reliability of the VRSUQ was evaluated through experiments that individually reported Cronbach's alpha values in the range of 0.679–0.896 (Table 4). The overall Cronbach's alpha values calculated for all participants fell between 0.752 and 0.773, satisfying the recommended standard for basic research of a reliability of 0.70 or higher (Nunnally, 1978). These results exceed the commonly required reliability standards at the initial stages of research, suggesting that the questionnaire is capable of reliably measuring user experience consistency across various VR systems.

4.2. Construct validity

It is necessary to measure the variables' characteristics to show validity in the construction of the questionnaire (Chow, 2002). To investigate construct validity in the VRSUQ, we performed EFA using principal axis factoring extraction with varimax rotation (Table 5). First, Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) and Bartlett's Test of Sphericity were conducted to check whether the data are suitable for factor analysis. As a result, the overall measure of sampling adequacy (MSA) was 0.820, which is acceptable. In addition, from Bartlett's test, the null hypothesis was rejected (Approx. Chi-square = 350.671, df = 36, p < 0.05), showing that the questionnaire meets the requirements for construct validity. EFA showed that the cumulative explanatory variance of each variable is over 50%, the overall measurement quality is good, and the questions are appropriate.

CFA was also used to determine the fit of the model obtained from EFA, yielding a Chi-square(24) = 29.682, p = 00.196. As a result, the values of the fitness indexes were confirmed to be within acceptable limits: Chi-square/df = 1.24 (acceptable level: <2; Carmines and McIver, 1981), goodness-of-fit index = 0.944 (acceptable level: >0.9; Tanaka and Huba, 1984), Tucker–Lewis index = 0.974 (acceptable level: >0.9; Bentler and Bonett, 1980), comparative fit index = 0.983 (acceptable level: >0.9; Bentler, 1990), and root mean square error of approximation = 0.048 (acceptable level: <0.08; Browne and Cudeck, 1993). Thus, we can conclude that the model was properly structured to account for the measured data.

4.3. Correspondence between the VRSUQ and SUS

The VRSUQ score was derived by referring to the formula corresponding to the SUS scores adopted in previous studies that developed perceived usability evaluation questionnaires based on SUS (Lewis et al., 2015; Lewis 2018a). SUS consists of five positive questions and five negative questions, and the score derived is between 0 and 100 points using the following procedure (Brooke, 1996). First, all scores are normalized to a scale of 0–4, in which one point is deducted for a positive question and points for negative questions are deducted from five points. Next, after calculating the sum of the normalized scores, the final SUS score can be obtained by multiplying the value by 2.5. The following formula calculates the SUS score and the VRSUQ score corresponding to SUS.

  • ●

    SUS = SUM((SUM(odd-numbered questions) – 5), (25 – SUM(even-numbered questions))) * 2.5

  • ●

    VRSUQ = (SUM(Physical discomfort, Pleasure, Emotional discomfort, Compatibility, Feedback, Error prevention, Understandability, Learnability, Error recovery)/9) – 1) * 100/4

To verify the convergent validity, we conducted a correlation analysis between the SUS scores and VRSUQ scores. The results of the correlation analysis for each experiment and the entire dataset are presented in Table 6. The correlation coefficients ranging from 0.745 to 0.835 indicate a strong positive correlation between the two variables. In this case, the significant level of correlation between SUS scores and VRSUQ scores suggests that the VRSUQ measures components similar to those assessed by the SUS. Therefore, these results demonstrate a high level of convergent validity, supporting the effectiveness of the VRSUQ as a valid tool for evaluating the usability of VR systems.

The VRSUQ scores were higher than the SUS scores and according to Sauro (2018), the average SUS score is 68, which is at the 50th percentile. Therefore, an SUS score above 68 is considered above average, while a score below 68 is considered below average. Based on the percentile ranges derived from large dataset of SUS scores, the SUS scores for the overall, E1, and E2 conditions fall within the percentile range of 41–59. For the E3 condition, the score falls within the percentile range of 60–64.

4.4. Comparative analysis of VRSUQ dimensions

A comparative analysis of scores across usability dimensions of VRSUQ was performed to provide practical methods for those assessing VR system usability. The RM-ANOVA results confirmed differences in the average scores among these dimensions for each VR system, as detailed in Table 7. For instance, in conditions E1, E2, and E3, the scores for the satisfaction dimension were higher than those for effectiveness, and in E3, there was a significant difference between the efficiency and satisfaction dimensions (Fig. 7). This suggests that users’ subjective satisfaction scores may have a more positive impact on the overall usability score (i.e., VRSUQ score) than other factors, and indicates the need for strategies to further improve usability in terms of effectiveness and efficiency.

5. Discussion

In this study, we developed and structured an evaluation tool to assess the usability of various categories of VR systems from a comprehensive perspective, reflecting the unique characteristics of VR systems, through systematic literature review and expert reviews. The proposed evaluation tool, the VRSUQ, was subjected to three separate user experiments to verify its reliability and validity. Results demonstrated satisfactory internal consistency and the construct validity of VRSUQ was confirmed through EFA and CFA. Furthermore, convergent validity was affirmed through correlation analysis with SUS scores, establishing that VRSUQ is a sufficiently suitable tool for assessing the usability of VR systems and can serve as a viable alternative to SUS.

As shown in Table 6, the usability of VR systems under the conditions E1, E2, and E3 resulted in SUS scores of 67.16, 60.33, and 71.95, respectively. The qualitative interpretation of these SUS scores has become possible through the collaborative efforts and interest of numerous researchers. For example, according to Sauro (2018), the average SUS score is 68, situating it at the 50th percentile. Consequently, an SUS score above 68 is regarded as above average, whereas a score below 68 is deemed below average. Drawing from the percentile ranges derived from a substantial dataset of SUS scores, the SUS scores for the overall, E1, and E2 conditions are positioned within the 41st to 59th percentile range. For the E3 condition, the score resides within the 60th to 64th percentile range. As the use of VRSUQ expands and its results continue to accumulate, we anticipate that percentile-based interpretations of VRSUQ scores will become feasible. Despite this, considering the high correlation coefficient with SUS scores, it can be inferred that VRSUQ demonstrates a comparable level of usability.

We conducted additional analysis beyond merely validating the reliability and validity of VRSUQ to enhance its practical application. This further analysis is intended to promote broader application and understanding of VRSUQ by providing practical insights on how to effectively utilize VRSUQ when evaluating VR system usability. Furthermore, compared to SUS, the usability evaluation using VRSUQ, which is structured around three dimensions of usability, enables more in-depth discussions about the usability scores of individual systems and provides deeper insights into the multifaceted nature of usability evaluation. In other words, the perceived usability of the VR system can be fully understood through the discussion of results from each detailed factor. For instance, based on the additional analysis results shown in Table 7 and Fig. 7., we can present the following key insights and discussion points.

Limited to the experimental results of this study, there is a primary need to enhance the effectiveness of VR systems. The usability indicators that constitute effectiveness include compatibility, feedback, and error prevention. Therefore, it is necessary to devise strategies ensuring user interactions with VR systems are met with expected responses, provide clear feedback on inputs, and prevent the occurrence of errors. Based on our observations of actual participants performing tasks in experiments, it is crucial to enable virtual navigation at a speed suitable for WIP behavior, and to make the method of changing direction using the thumb pad more intuitive (E1). In addition, when using an omnidirectional treadmill (E2), the friction was less than the experimenter expected, leading to a too slippery walking experience. This likely resulted in participants not receiving clear feedback on their actions, which in turn caused frequent errors in performing walking tasks correctly within the virtual environment. Moreover, in the case of E3, which involved many manipulation tasks, errors frequently occurred due to the physical structure of the HMD during the process of wearing virtual objects on the face, and they were not properly worn in the virtual environment. During tasks like opening a locker or throwing trash in a bin, cognitive mismatches in distance perception were observed compared to the participants’ expected distances. Although it was not the intent of this study to conduct systematic observations, we were able to identify issues and devise design improvement strategies by linking the evaluation results of each dimension of the VRSUQ with observational outcomes. Therefore, we anticipate that future usability evaluations of VR systems using this questionnaire, if accompanied by systematic observations, will facilitate more in-depth discussions and provide insights for problem-solving.

6. Conclusion

This study developed a perceived usability evaluation questionnaire, VRSUQ, for comprehensive usability evaluations suitable for VR systems, and experiments were conducted to prove the reliability and validity of the questionnaire. The VRSUQ consists of usability evaluation indicators that reflect the characteristics of VR applications, and the questionnaire consists of nine items. Therefore, we hope that experts or non-experts, and VR researchers or practitioners, can efficiently and effectively evaluate the perceived usability of VR systems by utilizing it. The VRSUQ is based on the core usability dimensions from the ISO, and has the advantage of being able to subdivide and discuss factors when proposing design guidelines by evaluating usability in more detail. The VRSUQ also allows identifying and discussing usability issues that are difficult to address with SUS alone. For example, the VRSUQ focuses on VR experiences that are not covered in SUS. Therefore, problems such as dizziness or mental strain cannot be identified with SUS but can be identified with the VRSUQ. Additionally, the VRSUQ includes questions about the system's response time, clarity in feedback, and ease of error correction, which are not covered in SUS. These questions provide more specific insights into usability in the VR context.

Nevertheless, the discussion of reliability and validity should continue, as the results of using this questionnaire on a variety of VR platforms with users of different demographics will help us understand the characteristics of VR systems and how demographics affect the usability of VR systems. Furthermore, we aim to enhance the reliability of the VRSUQ scale by actively promoting its use and providing accessible evaluation templates through online forms. This approach is intended to facilitate researchers in easily applying the VRSUQ scale across various contexts, thereby validating its applicability and increasing its credibility. Although this study focused on developing the VRSUQ and suggesting possibilities for using it, it is expected that it will be widely used as a more powerful and robust VR-specific, perceived usability evaluation tool when the results of using the VRSUQ are accumulated owing to interest from various related researchers.
